clue.text: Marston's Duke, and largely malevolent fool ()

definitions.text: Marston's Duke, and largely malevolent fool

parts.words: Marston's Duke, and largely malevolent fool
parts.note: in John Marston's play The Malcontent the deposed duke disguises himself as Malevole, a railing jester whose name is most of the word malevolent

explanation.surface: A theatre note on a Jacobean duke who is mostly spite and partly clown.
explanation.walkthrough: The deposed Duke Altofronto of this Italian city goes about in The Malcontent as Malevole, a bitter fool; 'largely malevolent' points at that name, which is malevolent minus its end.
explanation.definitionFit: The duke's title in Marston's play is taken from the Italian port city he rules.

clue.text: Ledger now revised for Shrewsbury absentee

indicators.note: revised says the letters of ledger now are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: An account book is redone for a man who missed a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges LEDGERNOW. In Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 the Welsh rebel fails to arrive for the Battle of Shrewsbury.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh leader Owen did not bring his forces to the 1403 battle, so he was the one missing there.

clue.text: Innocent, like John le Carré' lover

explanation.surface: A spy novelist's sweetheart is described as guileless.
explanation.definitionFit: Innocent means unworldly and trusting; le Carré's novel is The Naive and Sentimental Lover, so his lover is so described.

clue.text: Bunyan's Destroyer shows no return support for a communicative pet

indicators.note: in a down answer a piece placed beneath others holds them up, so it comes last

parts.note: Polly is the stock name for a talking parrot

indicators.note: return asks for the word no to be read the other way round

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned

explanation.surface: A Puritan's destroying demon somehow refuses to back a talking parrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no return' turns NO into ON, and 'support for' puts that ON under A POLLY in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollyon is the fiend Christian fights in The Pilgrim's Progress; the name means destroyer in Greek.

clue.text: One of Fleming's smaller canvases

parts.note: Fleming suggests the painter or scientist, but it is Ian Fleming's Bond novel, also the name of a small light sail high on a mast

explanation.surface: An art catalogue note on a modest painting by an artist called Fleming.
explanation.walkthrough: Canvases suggests paintings; in sailing, canvas means sail, and this is a tiny sail set above the skysail, as well as an Ian Fleming title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bond book is named after a small topmost sail, and sail is the sailor's sense of canvas.

clue.text: Jamaican novelist, but French

explanation.surface: A Caribbean writer is introduced with a French conjunction.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Mais was a Jamaican novelist (Brother Man); the French word for but is spelt the same.

clue.text: Byron was always looking in mirrors to make sure he was sufficiently so, said Enoch Powell

definitions.text: Byron was always looking in mirrors to make sure he was sufficiently so, said Enoch Powell

parts.words: Byron was always looking in mirrors to make sure he was sufficiently so, said Enoch Powell
parts.note: a remark of the politician Enoch Powell about the vain, scandalous poet: so stands for a word meaning shocking

explanation.surface: A politician's quip about the poet's vanity before the looking glass.
explanation.walkthrough: Enoch Powell was a British Conservative politician and classical scholar; the missing word is the quality Byron checked for in the mirror.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's public image was deliberately shocking and scandalous, which the word describes.

clue.text: Possibly desperate in Hardy's case

parts.note: Thomas Hardy's first novel is Desperate Remedies, so in his case the thing that was desperate is a cure, in the singular

explanation.surface: A remark that a man called Hardy may be in a desperate state.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy's case reads like a patient's condition, but it means his book title, Desperate Remedies; the light wants that noun in the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: A cure or treatment can be desperate, a last resort, as in Hardy's title.

clue.text: Most amiable character isn't liked somehow

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of isn't liked are put together in some other way

explanation.surface: A person whose character is pleasant yet is not liked, for reasons unclear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges ISNTLIKED; 'character' joins the definition to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Kind and amiable are near synonyms for good-natured, so the superlatives match.

clue.text: Radical start of Kunta Kinta

parts.note: radical comes from the Latin for the underground part of a plant, and Alex Haley's saga of Kunta Kinte's family origins bears that title

explanation.surface: The fiery political beginnings of a character in an African American saga.
explanation.walkthrough: Radical comes from Latin radix, so a radical start is where things grow from; Haley's book tracing Kunta Kinte (printed Kinta) has that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancestral origins are a family's source, the underground part from which it grows.

clue.text: Blurb-writer converted to pietism

indicators.note: converted says the letters of to pietism are changed into a new form

explanation.surface: A copywriter is said to have taken up a devout religious movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' looks religious beside pietism, but it rearranges TOPIETISM.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes summaries condenses a book into a short account, which is what blurbs do.

clue.text: Dream of park explorer revealed by Stewart

definitions.text: Dream of park explorer revealed by Stewart

parts.words: Dream of park explorer revealed by Stewart
parts.note: J I M Stewart wrote the novel ... Dream, and the Scottish explorer of the Niger was ... Park

explanation.surface: A writer named Stewart discloses what a traveller in a park dreamt.
explanation.walkthrough: Park is the surname of the Scottish explorer of West Africa; the light is his first name, which is also in J I M Stewart's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The explorer's forename appears in the possessive in Stewart's novel title about a dream.

clue.text: "The man who —— upon himself … rests in his true centre " (Donne)

definitions.text: "The man who —— upon himself … rests in his true centre " (Donne)

parts.words: "The man who —— upon himself … rests in his true centre " (Donne)
parts.note: a quotation from John Donne with one verb missing, meaning lives or stays

explanation.surface: A line from Donne about a self-contained man at rest in himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means abides or resides, fitting a man at home in his own centre.

clue.text: His work concealed a lot of bull

definitions.text: His work concealed a lot of bull

parts.words: His work concealed a lot of bull
parts.note: in Greek myth the craftsman built the Labyrinth that hid the Minotaur, a monster half bull

explanation.surface: A jibe that someone's output hid a great deal of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A lot of bull reads as nonsense; it is the Minotaur, kept in the maze the Athenian inventor built for King Minos.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical Athenian inventor built the Labyrinth, so his work hid the bull-headed monster.

clue.text: Pistol's mad version of musical arranger

indicators.note: a version of something is another form of it, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Pistol, gone crazy, offers his take on a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' rearranges PISTOLSMAD; Pistol is Falstaff's swaggering companion in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: One who sets psalms to music is a composer or arranger of sacred song.

clue.text: Novelist from port in Osborne play?

parts.note: Rebecca West, the British novelist
of can mean from, as in a man of Kent
Suez is the Egyptian port on its canal

explanation.surface: A writer from a harbour town appears in a John Osborne play.
explanation.walkthrough: John Osborne was the English playwright of Look Back in Anger; the question mark marks the title as a phrase built from pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: John Osborne wrote a 1971 play with this title about a British colony after empire.

clue.text: A number noticed around occurrence by Tarkington

indicators.note: around says one word is put about the other

parts.note: noticed means seen
an occurrence is an event

explanation.surface: A tally spotted near some incident in a Booth Tarkington book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by Tarkington' adds that the number is also the title of Booth Tarkington's 1916 novel of adolescence.
explanation.definitionFit: Seventeen is a cardinal, a figure, and the title of Tarkington's 1916 novel.

clue.text: Snare, say, for Wilder's Emily

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken and only its sound counts

parts.note: a web is a snare, as a spider's is

explanation.surface: A trap set for a young woman in a Thornton Wilder play.
explanation.walkthrough: Emily is the heroine of Thornton Wilder's Our Town.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily's surname in Our Town is the one heard here.

clue.text: Esmond's beneficent Baroness Beatrix

parts.note: Beatrix, the heroine of Thackeray's Henry Esmond, later appears in The Virginians as a German baroness who aids her young kin

explanation.surface: A kindly titled lady from Thackeray's historical novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Thackeray's Beatrix Esmond marries a German nobleman and, as the elderly baroness in The Virginians, helps her young American relation.
explanation.definitionFit: The baroness's married title in The Virginians is the name of her German husband.

clue.text: "A pool called… , having five porches" (St John's Gospel)

definitions.text: "A pool called… , having five porches" (St John's Gospel)

parts.words: "A pool called… , having five porches" (St John's Gospel)
parts.note: John 5:2 names the healing pool in Jerusalem by the sheep market

explanation.surface: A line from John's Gospel about a pool ringed with porches.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospel names the pool in Jerusalem where Jesus healed the lame man.

clue.text: Wander, like Mrs Behn's Willmore?

explanation.surface: Someone drifts aimlessly, as a character from a Restoration play did.
explanation.walkthrough: Aphra Behn's play The Rover has Willmore as its title character; the question mark marks that he does this as his calling.
explanation.definitionFit: To wander is to roam about; Willmore is Behn's Rover, a man who roams.

clue.text: Potter's tailor's place

parts.note: Beatrix Potter wrote The Tailor of ..., named for the English cathedral city

explanation.surface: Where a potter's dressmaker sets up shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Potter suggests a craftsman with clay; it is Beatrix Potter, whose tailor lives in an English cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: The city in the West of England is the home of the tailor in Potter's tale.

clue.text: Stoical Iroquois philosopher?

parts.note: one name fits both a Roman Stoic thinker and a nation of the Iroquois confederacy

explanation.surface: A Native American sage who bears hardship calmly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman Stoic who tutored Nero shares his name with one of the six Iroquois nations of New York state.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to Nero's Stoic tutor and to an Iroquois people.

clue.text: Son of Ban from Percy (and Percy)

explanation.surface: A king's son drawn from two writers named Percy.
explanation.walkthrough: Walker Percy wrote a novel with this title, and Bishop Thomas Percy's Reliques includes a ballad of the same knight.
explanation.definitionFit: King Ban of Benwick was the father of the Round Table knight, the subject of both Percys' works.

clue.text: Orientalist seen in nearly all his own books

indicators.note: seen in says the answer is visible inside the words nearly all

explanation.surface: A scholar of the East whose name appears on almost all his own titles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' finds the name across nearly all; 'his own books' adds that an author's name is on most of his books.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Charles Lyall was a British scholar of Arabic poetry, an expert on the East.

clue.text: Doubting Rhymer?

explanation.surface: A sceptical versifier.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle who doubted the resurrection and the Scottish seer called the Rhymer share this name.

clue.text: Shakespearean dream queen with the Spanish girl

parts.note: Queen Mab brings dreams in Mercutio's speech in Romeo and Juliet
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A fairy queen from Shakespeare is joined by a young woman from Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name stands for a girl in crosswords.

clue.text: England is for it, said Beryl Bainbridge

definitions.text: England is for it, said Beryl Bainbridge

parts.words: England is for it, said Beryl Bainbridge
parts.note: Beryl Bainbridge wrote the travel book ... England, so in her title England stands just after the word for

explanation.surface: A novelist declares that England is in for trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For it' sounds like England being in trouble; it means the word that comes after for in Bainbridge's title Forever England.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means always, and with for it makes the phrase meaning eternally in her title.

clue.text: Julia Kavanagh novel discovered among some low-grade lettres ()

indicators.note: discovered among some says the answer is a run of letters found inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A Victorian novel turns up in a pile of second-rate literature.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'discovered among' into the definition; it belongs with 'some' as the signal, leaving 'Julia Kavanagh novel' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Julia Kavanagh, an Irish Victorian novelist, published the novel Adèle in 1858.

clue.text: Means of support lacking for an atheist, according to John Buchan

definitions.text: Means of support lacking for an atheist, according to John Buchan

parts.words: Means of support lacking for an atheist, according to John Buchan
parts.note: Buchan's quip: an atheist is a man who has no unseen means of support

explanation.surface: A novelist's verdict on how an unbeliever gets by.
explanation.walkthrough: John Buchan, author of The Thirty-Nine Steps, defined an atheist as a man with no such means of support, playing on the phrase for income that cannot be seen.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means unseen, as God is, and appears in the phrase for unexplained income.

clue.text: Time-honoured bomber? (somewhat emaciated)

parts.note: Shakespeare's Richard II opens with old John of Gaunt, time-honoured, and gaunt means emaciated; the name is also a wartime RAF aircraft

explanation.surface: A venerable old warplane that has grown rather thin.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard II opens 'Old John of Gaunt, time-honour'd' with this title; gaunt means emaciated, and the same name was a Second World War RAF heavy bomber.
explanation.definitionFit: John of Gaunt was Duke of the northern county, and an Avro bomber bore the same name.

clue.text: Maiden name of Arabella Winklepicker?

parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers Arabella elopes with Mr Winkle, so she picked Winkle; a winklepicker is also a pointed shoe

explanation.surface: The birth surname of a woman called after a pointed shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: Winklepicker is British slang for a sharply pointed 1950s shoe; here it means she chose Mr Winkle in The Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Before marrying Winkle, Dickens's Arabella bore her brother Benjamin's surname.
